sources.title: Tragedy and Hope: A History of the World in Our Time
sources.author: Carroll Quigley
sources.description: A wide-ranging historical synthesis of financial capitalism, imperial administration, international diplomacy, world wars and the Cold War. This supplied PDF is a retyped, annotated edition rather than a facsimile of the 1966 printing. Accounts distinguish Quigley’s interpretations from the later introduction and visible editorial insertions.
sources.pageConvention: All citations use 1-based pages of this 1,090-page PDF. These are not page numbers in the original Macmillan printing. January 1 and the first of a month are plotting anchors for dates whose day is not given.
sources.coverage: Selective, substantive extraction across the book’s institutional and political chapters, with emphasis on finance, empire and connections through the 1950s; selected 1960s developments extend the chronology. This is not an exhaustive index of every name, battle or theoretical passage. Selected institutional, financial and imperial passages in chapters 5–14 (PDF pages 47–229), with particular attention to banking mechanisms, Rhodes–Milner affiliations, constitutional reforms and the diplomatic origins of the First World War. Civilizational theory and passing references are not exhaustively indexed. Additional selected pages158–186 address foreign customs supervision, Japan’s political-economic organization and Chinese republican instability. Substantial reading of PDF pages 230–307, 399–417, and 449–454 within chapters 15–38, concentrating on the Versailles settlement, collective security, reparations, central-bank cooperation, stabilization and the 1931 crisis, British political institutions and labor, and the New Deal. This is a selective event-and-network digest, not an exhaustive transcription of every country chapter. PDF pages 472–792, chapters 39–65: Japanese and Italian aggression, British appeasement and institutional networks, European war, Allied strategy and postwar institutions, atomic diplomacy, and Cold War formation through 1950. The supplied PDF contains bracketed editorial interpolations; this digest does not attribute those additions to Quigley. Dates retain the precision supported by the supplied text, and known internal date inconsistencies are identified rather than silently repaired. Substantive reading of PDF pages 793–994, covering nuclear strategy, Korea, Eisenhower institutions, Soviet succession, Iran, Suez, Cuba, and Asian/African decolonization; selected late-book analysis pp 1011,1031–1034 and concluding 1963–1964 developments pp 1088–1090. Summaries exclude recognizable bracketed editorial interpolations. Citations use PDF page numbers, not printed-page labels.

Oglesby regards the contrast between his public Marxist identity and these relationships as a reason to question the official biography; his proposed covert assignment remains unconfirmed.

events.name: Cuban Missile Crisis intensifies internal disputes
events.description: The missile confrontation increased pressure on Kennedy to act militarily against Cuba. Oglesby argues that the settlement also deepened conflict with anti-Castro militants because American assurances about Cuba’s security required restraining raids. His discussion of a possible military overthrow relies on a reported memoir account, not an established coup attempt.

events.name: Kennedy proposes ending oil-depletion allowance
events.description: Kennedy’s proposed removal of the oil-depletion allowance threatened a major source of the Southwestern oil industry’s profits. Oglesby includes the proposal in his catalogue of conflicts with Texas interests and argues that it contributed to hostility toward the administration; any connection to an assassination motive is his interpretation.

events.description: Kennedy’s announcement that American-based raids on Cuba would cease angered exile militants, according to a Miami police intelligence report cited by Oglesby. The author presents the shift as an enforcement consequence of Kennedy’s Cuba policy and a source of domestic hostility, rather than merely a change in military tactics.

events.description: Oswald’s move to New Orleans brings his public pro-Castro activity into contact with the anti-Castro networks central to Oglesby’s argument. events.description: A confrontation while Oswald distributed pro-Castro leaflets led to his arrest in New Orleans. Oglesby emphasizes that Oswald asked to speak to the FBI and was released after a small fine, using the episode to challenge the assumption that his public political identity explained all of his activities.

events.name: Federal raids close anti-Castro camps
events.description: Federal action against anti-Castro camps in Florida and Louisiana restricted raids that Kennedy’s government sought to stop. Oglesby connects the closures to the aftermath of the missile settlement and to anger among former invasion supporters, while treating alleged links involving Ferrie, Sturgis and Ruby’s associates as elements of his reconstruction.

events.name: Oswald’s reported Mexico City visit
events.description: The book examines the reported Mexico City trip and CIA messages about embassy contacts, stressing discrepancies between surveillance descriptions and Oswald’s appearance. Oglesby raises impersonation as an explanation and compares other disputed sightings; the material presented here does not resolve whether each reported contact involved Oswald or another person.

events.name: McNamara announces planned troop withdrawal
events.description: McNamara announced a plan to withdraw one thousand American personnel from Vietnam before the end of 1963. Oglesby places the announcement within a broader claimed disengagement strategy and contrasts it with later escalation. His inference that Kennedy had settled on long-term withdrawal goes beyond the limited personnel announcement itself.

events.name: Diem government overthrown
events.description: The Diem government was overthrown and Diem and Nhu were killed. Oglesby distinguishes Kennedy’s approval of a change in government from uncertainty over responsibility for the murders, arguing that the coup belonged to a potential negotiating strategy. He also questions later efforts by Hunt to portray Kennedy as authorizing the killings.

events.name: Cherami encountered on Louisiana roadside
events.description: Rose Cherami was found injured near Eunice, Louisiana, and passed through police and hospital custody before Kennedy’s assassination. Oglesby repeats accounts that she later spoke of Ruby, Oswald and advance knowledge of the killing. These statements come through investigators and medical witnesses and do not independently establish foreknowledge or a conspiracy.

events.name: Kennedy assassinated at Dealey Plaza
events.description: Kennedy was killed and Governor Connally wounded during the Dallas motorcade. Oglesby reviews the Warren Commission’s lone-Oswald explanation, challenges its shooting reconstruction and argues for a political coup interpretation. The assassination and injuries are distinct from his contested conclusions about shooters, sponsors and the policy objectives of a hidden group.

events.name: Ruby kills Oswald in police custody
events.description: Ruby shot Oswald during his transfer from the Dallas city jail, eliminating the possibility of a trial of the accused assassin. Oglesby contrasts Ruby’s stated wish to spare Jacqueline Kennedy another ordeal with his criminal and police contacts, but the author’s proposed conspiracy motive is not established by the shooting alone.

events.name: Commission privately discusses Oswald and FBI
events.description: A private Warren Commission discussion examined suspicions about Oswald’s FBI contacts and the bureau’s handling of leads. Oglesby cites a transcript released through Harold Weisberg’s litigation, interpreting the commissioners’ concerns as evidence that institutional obstruction was visible during the investigation. Suspicions discussed in the meeting were not findings that Oswald was an informant.

events.name: Commission discusses alleged Oswald informer ties
events.description: The commission considered an allegation that Oswald received FBI payments and discussed the difficulty of proving a secret intelligence relationship. Oglesby uses the exchange to challenge a categorical denial of covert ties, but inability to disprove a confidential relationship does not establish that the alleged payments or employment existed.

events.name: Connally disputes shared-bullet account
events.description: Connally said he believed the shot that wounded him was different from the first shot that struck Kennedy. Oglesby treats that testimony as a challenge to the shared-bullet reconstruction, placing the governor’s perception beside timing and wound arguments. The testimony records Connally’s experience; it does not alone resolve the full trajectory analysis.

events.name: Ruby testifies to Warren and Ford
events.description: Ruby asked Warren and Ford for a lie-detector test and transfer to Washington, saying he could not give a satisfactory account under his Dallas circumstances. Oglesby reads his fragmented warnings as potentially significant, but the testimony’s ambiguity, Ruby’s mental condition and competing interpretations prevent it from establishing the larger conspiracy the author proposes.

events.name: Hoover reports neutron-activation comparisons
events.description: Hoover’s letter addressed neutron-activation comparisons of lead fragments relevant to the assassination reconstruction. Oglesby uses the reported results to challenge claims that the fragments established a common bullet origin. His categorical conclusions about the forensic implications are part of the book’s argument and require separate scientific assessment.

events.name: Ruby undergoes lengthy FBI polygraph
events.description: Ruby underwent a lengthy FBI polygraph session after requesting testing during his commission testimony. Oglesby highlights the presence of people Ruby distrusted, the duration and the examiner’s concerns about fatigue, arguing that the results could not reliably settle questions of motive or conspiracy. The test did not provide conclusive proof of either account.

events.name: SDS organizes national antiwar march
events.description: Students for a Democratic Society organized a Washington antiwar demonstration drawing roughly twenty to twenty-five thousand people in the book’s account. Speakers from SDS and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee called for a mass movement against the Vietnam War, marking public opposition alongside the policy and establishment conflicts Oglesby traces.

events.name: Cherami dies in Texas road incident
events.description: Cherami died following a road collision near Big Sandy, Texas. Oglesby reproduces investigators’ doubts about the circumstances while noting that the case was closed as accidental. The passage reconnects the deceased woman with the earlier Louisiana witness account but does not establish that her death was murder or connected to her statements.

Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Kilgallen dies before developing assassination lead
events.description: Dorothy Kilgallen died before publishing a lead she had told associates could transform the Kennedy case. Oglesby notes her earlier access to Ruby and the disappearance of her case notes. The death was ruled an accidental alcohol-and-barbiturate overdose; the passage’s unresolved questions do not establish an assassination-related killing.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.

events.name: Ruby dies in custody
events.description: Ruby died while in custody after serious illness. Oglesby records his claim that he was being poisoned and places the death alongside the unfinished questions about his testimony. The book’s reporting of Ruby’s suspicion should remain separate from the illness and death, because it does not establish deliberate poisoning.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Gold-outflow crisis affects Vietnam policy debate
events.description: The gold-outflow crisis exposed the international economic costs of the Vietnam War in Oglesby’s account. He argues that Atlantic-oriented financial interests became less willing to sustain escalation, while others saw continued commitment as essential. The crisis sharpened policy division but did not automatically determine one common response among business or political leaders.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Johnson withdraws from presidential race
events.description: Johnson’s decision not to seek another term and his movement toward negotiations are interpreted by Oglesby as a successful establishment challenge to escalation. He connects the shift with Tet, economic strain and advisers such as Clifford, Harriman, Vance and Ball. His claim of a clandestine power play remains an interpretation of the political transition.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: King assassinated
events.description: King’s killing is followed in the book by disputes over eyewitness accounts, shooting position and James Earl Ray’s legal defense. Oglesby argues that the lone-Ray explanation required renewed investigation. His presentation includes contested claims and Ray’s later assertions; it should not be treated as a completed finding about additional participants.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Hoover issues New Left counterintelligence memos
events.description: Hoover’s May memoranda directed FBI offices to expose, disrupt and neutralize New Left organizations and leadership. Oglesby sees the program as a state campaign against civil-rights and antiwar politics. He acknowledges that its full scope and impact were not known to him, despite drawing a strong connection to the movement’s decline.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Robert Kennedy assassination disrupts election coalition
events.description: Robert Kennedy’s assassination ended a potential antiwar electoral coalition, in Oglesby’s interpretation. The chapter questions shooting direction, bullet comparisons and handling of physical evidence, while arguing that Humphrey’s subsequent ascendancy preserved the existing foreign-policy course. The forensic allegations and the claim of a hidden political design remain contested source arguments.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Nixon discusses Bay of Pigs during Watergate cover-up
events.description: Nixon’s recorded discussions with Haldeman used the Bay of Pigs and Hunt’s knowledge while seeking to contain the Watergate investigation. Oglesby asks what undisclosed connections the language implied. The tapes document discussion of obstruction and intelligence associations; his proposed deeper link among Cuba, Nixon and later political crimes remains a hypothesis.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Hughes accepts TWA financing and voting trust
events.description: Hughes accepted financing arrangements that transferred effective control of TWA away from him. Oglesby presents the transaction as the outcome of pressure by lenders rather than a voluntary retreat by an eccentric owner. The event begins the prolonged litigation and loss-of-control sequence that later sharpened divisions inside the Hughes organization.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Hughes divests TWA stock, in book’s dating
events.description: Hughes sold his controlling TWA holding after years of litigation. Oglesby emphasizes the enormous cash proceeds and describes the divestment as a defeat that also funded his move into Nevada gambling. The archive preserves the book’s stated date rather than independently certifying the transaction’s chronology.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Hughes takes residence at Desert Inn
events.description: Hughes moved into the Desert Inn penthouse prepared by Robert Maheu, beginning four years of Nevada expansion. Oglesby portrays the arrival as a secret entry into a gambling economy dominated by criminal interests, with Maheu supplying security and management. The author’s description of an eventual struggle with Lansky is his interpretation.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Maheu memo discusses hiring Kennedy aides
events.description: Maheu’s memo arranged an employment discussion with Larry O’Brien shortly after Robert Kennedy’s death. O’Brien’s firm subsequently consulted for Hughes, but Oglesby could not determine its full duties. He considers whether access to Hughes–Nixon information might help explain later interest in the Democratic headquarters, while leaving that motive unproven.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Maheu receives authority over TWA litigation
events.description: Hughes gave Maheu broad responsibility for resolving the TWA litigation, and the Toolco directors formally confirmed that authority. Oglesby presents the assignment as both a promotion and a danger: it brought the Nevada manager directly into conflict with Chester Davis, who had controlled the legal strategy and retained his corporate position.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Metzner awards damages against Hughes
events.description: Judge Metzner entered a judgment exceeding $145 million against Hughes, increasing pressure on Maheu to find a new legal strategy. Oglesby explains that expenses later raised the exposure toward $160 million before the Supreme Court rejected the case’s jurisdictional basis. The judgment intensified an existing organizational rivalry rather than creating it.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Contested proxy grants Toolco authority
events.description: A short proxy, said to bear Hughes’s signature, gave the Toolco board power to act for him. Its existence became decisive in Maheu’s removal, but opposing handwriting experts later disagreed about authenticity. Oglesby situates the document inside a wider battle over control of the secluded owner’s communications and personal attendants.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Hughes leaves Las Vegas for Bahamas
events.description: Hughes left the Desert Inn secretly and traveled to the Bahamas through Nellis Air Force Base. Oglesby calls the surrounding transfer of power a Thanksgiving coup, emphasizing that Maheu’s security organization remained unaware. He asks whether Nixon-connected security executive James Golden implies political involvement, but presents that connection as an unresolved question.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Las Vegas Sun reports Hughes missing
events.description: The Las Vegas Sun reported Hughes missing after Greenspun and Maheu learned the penthouse had become unexpectedly quiet. Oglesby traces how the headline was then used in the dispute over Maheu’s loyalty, relying on aides’ accounts of Hughes’s reaction. The episode shows public reporting becoming an instrument in an internal corporate struggle.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Toolco formally dismisses Maheu
events.description: Davis told Maheu’s lawyer Edward Morgan that Toolco had formally fired his client, displaying the proxy as proof of authority. Oglesby describes the meeting as the public completion of a struggle already shaped by restricted communications and Hughes’s removal to the Bahamas. Claims of poor performance were part of the board’s position.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Proxy presented in control dispute
events.description: The contested proxy reached court together with a letter purportedly supporting Davis. The judge accepted the handwriting evidence supporting Hughes’s signature, leaving Maheu without his job. Oglesby reports the ruling while continuing to question the owner’s isolation and whether the board or Hughes was the effective author of the change.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Meeting plans Greenspun document burglary
events.description: A meeting connected Mullen executive Robert Bennett, Hunt and new Hughes security chief Ralph Winte around their interest in Maheu’s papers held by Greenspun. Oglesby recounts a burglary plan and proposed escape logistics through Watergate testimony. An actual safe-opening attempt was reported later, but its connection to the Plumbers was never conclusively established.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Entry team arrested at Watergate
events.description: The second Watergate entry ended in arrests after tape on a door latch alerted security. Oglesby assembles testimony that McCord favored proceeding despite an earlier discovery of tape and failed to remove it. He interprets the sequence as deliberate exposure by a double agent; McCord denied a conspiracy to reveal the Plumbers.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: McCord recounts Caulfield clemency offer
events.description: McCord recounted a July meeting in which Caulfield offered clemency, a limited prison term and financial support. Oglesby argues that McCord’s refusal to accept a defense blaming the CIA kept the scandal from being contained. The offer and refusal are presented through McCord’s account, while the claimed strategic consequence is the author’s judgment.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: McCord writes Helms about CIA-blame narrative
events.description: McCord wrote Helms about efforts to portray Watergate as a CIA operation and about alternative allegations against the defendants. Oglesby treats the personal correspondence as evidence that McCord remained closely aligned with agency interests after arrest. Correspondence establishes contact and advocacy, but does not itself prove a continuing covert assignment.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: McCord recounts trial-silence discussion
events.description: McCord described Alch discussing silence at trial, clemency and financial assistance after visiting Hunt’s lawyer Bittman. McCord said he had stopped taking Dorothy Hunt’s money because it appeared to be a control mechanism. Oglesby uses the lunch to explain tensions within the defense and cover-up; Alch later disputed the alleged false-CIA-defense proposal.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: United Flight 553 crashes at Chicago Midway
events.description: United Flight 553 crashed near Chicago Midway, killing Dorothy Hunt and other passengers. Oglesby challenges aspects of the official crew-error account and explores claims of sabotage tied to Watergate. The chapter also records official explanations and critiques of those allegations; the material does not establish that the crash was a planned killing.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Krogh moved to transportation department
events.description: Krogh’s sudden appointment to the Department of Transportation followed the Flight 553 crash by a day in Oglesby’s chronology. The author finds the timing and Krogh’s prior role organizing the White House investigative unit significant, arguing that the move placed a Nixon operative near the investigation. Timing alone does not establish intervention in the accident.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Butterfield announced as FAA administrator
events.description: Butterfield was announced as the next FAA administrator after the crash, but his appointment was delayed because the position restricted military officers. Oglesby links the move to Butterfield’s White House and intelligence-liaison background and interprets it as part of a potentially significant reshuffling around the aviation investigation.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: McCord warns Gaynor about blaming CIA
events.description: McCord warned CIA officer Paul Gaynor that pressure was building to assign responsibility for Watergate to the agency. He suggested newspaper leaks or anonymous letters exposing that plan before it hardened. Oglesby reads the correspondence as active tactical coordination; the text more directly establishes McCord’s effort to protect the CIA narrative.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: McCord discusses timing disclosures
events.description: A further McCord letter to Gaynor discussed possessing evidence against Mitchell and others and holding it until the trial for maximum effect. Oglesby regards this as advance planning for the disclosures that later transformed Watergate. The tactical language establishes a wish to time revelations, while a covert institutional command remains the author’s inference.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Supreme Court reverses Hughes antitrust case
events.description: The Supreme Court accepted the jurisdictional argument Davis had advanced for Hughes and rejected the antitrust case’s court route. Oglesby presents the decision as belated vindication after divestment and enormous damages exposure. The legal outcome supports the regulatory argument without necessarily proving every claim that bankers conspired to dispossess Hughes.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Flight 553 public hearings open
events.description: Public hearings into Flight 553 opened in Chicago while disputes over safety-board administration were intensifying. Oglesby notes Chapin’s attendance after joining United and connects the hearings with Miller’s conflict over Spears’s management. The hearings provided an official venue, but alternative investigators complained that their arguments were excluded.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Skolnick seeks testimony at crash hearings
events.description: Skolnick asked the Flight 553 board of inquiry for an opportunity to present his allegations in public session. Oglesby says chair Isobel Burgess rejected the petition immediately. The refusal becomes part of the author’s criticism of investigative openness, while it does not independently validate the sabotage theory Skolnick wanted to present.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Skolnick sues over crash hearings
events.description: After his petition was rejected, Skolnick filed a Cook County suit against inquiry chair Burgess and denounced the crash hearings. Oglesby presents the legal action as an escalation of the disagreement over access to the investigation. Filing the suit records a challenge to procedure, not a court finding that sabotage occurred.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Bottos detained for mental observation
events.description: Bottos was taken for mental observation at a federal facility, according to Oglesby, shortly before the Sarelli prosecution concluded without his testimony. Bottos believed the detention prevented disclosure of a crash-related link. Prosecutor Peter Vaira instead explained that the government avoided calling him because his testimony could become uncontrolled and confusing.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: McCord sends letter to Judge Sirica
events.description: McCord’s letter to Judge Sirica disrupted efforts to contain the Watergate case and identified pressure and political involvement beyond the arrested entry team. Oglesby treats it as the decisive shift from scandal to presidential crisis, connecting it with McCord’s earlier correspondence about timing disclosures. A broader covert mission remains an interpretation.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Krogh resigns DOT post
events.description: Krogh resigned his transportation post after exposure of his involvement in the Fielding burglary. Oglesby places the resignation amid questions about influence over the safety board, illustrating how the White House investigative unit’s activities reached officials holding responsibility near the crash inquiry. The resignation itself does not establish interference with the crash findings.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Alch denies proposed false CIA defense
events.description: Alch denied proposing that McCord falsely attribute Watergate to the CIA and rejected the allegation that agency records could be forged for that defense. He also questioned McCord’s relationship with Fensterwald. Oglesby uses the testimony to explore a prior connection, while reporting that its nature and significance remained disputed.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: IRS seeks Maheu material from Greenspun
events.description: Two IRS agents sought Maheu’s material from Greenspun shortly after testimony about the proposed document burglary became public. Oglesby says Greenspun obtained court protection and retained the papers. The author interprets the approach as continuing White House interest, but the cited sequence does not prove that the IRS acted on a presidential order.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: NTSB asks FBI to explain early crash actions
events.description: NTSB chairman Reed asked the FBI to explain agents’ early and unusual actions after the Flight 553 crash. His letter identified interviews and listening to control-tower tapes before safety investigators acted, and sought records and a clearer division of responsibility. Oglesby uses it to support concerns about investigative overlap, not as proof of sabotage.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: FBI explains response to Flight 553
events.description: Ruckelshaus replied that the FBI investigated potential federal aircraft crimes, initially did not know Dorothy Hunt was aboard and ended its inquiry after finding no apparent violation. He reported roughly fifty agents and first arrival within forty-five minutes. Oglesby questions the scale and timing, but those questions do not disprove the official explanation.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: NTSB issues final Flight 553 report
events.description: The NTSB’s final report attributed Flight 553’s crash to crew handling and loss of aircraft control; Oglesby’s appendix challenges its reconstruction. He focuses on the failed flight-data recorder, spoilers, altimeter behavior and cockpit responses. Disagreement with the official explanation does not establish the sabotage mechanism proposed by outside investigators.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Trilateral Commission formed
events.description: Rockefeller formed the Trilateral Commission on Brzezinski’s advice, according to Oglesby, to articulate shared interests among North America, Western Europe and Japan. The author connects it to older establishment networks and resistance to economic nationalism. Those network and faction descriptions are his analytical interpretation rather than proof of a formal parent-body relationship.

history.note: Added from yankee; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Maheu wins libel verdict
events.description: Maheu won a jury verdict against Hughes over accusations that he was dishonest and had stolen from his employer. Oglesby presents the result as supporting Maheu’s defense after years of investigation failed to substantiate the board’s allegations. The verdict concerns those defamatory charges, not every wider claim about Hughes’s removal or criminal networks.

Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Carter appoints Trilateral members
events.description: Carter appointed numerous Trilateral members to senior positions and had chosen Mondale as running mate. Oglesby interprets the concentration as evidence that organized establishment support helped shape the new administration. He allows for Carter’s own populism and coalition-building, so the account should not reduce membership overlap to proof that the commission directed every decision.
